segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set you free from the law of sin and death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For what the law could not do, weak as it was through the flesh, God did: sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and as a sin offering, he condemned sin in the flesh,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, on the things of the Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the mindset of the flesh is death, but the mindset of the Spirit is life and peace,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because the mindset of the flesh is hostility toward God; for it does not submit to God’s law, nor indeed can it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. And if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if Christ is in you, though the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit who dwells in you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, brothers and sisters, we are debtors—not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if you live according to the flesh, you are going to die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you did not receive a spirit of slavery, to fall back into fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry out,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Abba, Father!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if children, then heirs—heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I consider that the sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is going to be revealed to us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the creation was subjected to futility—not willingly, but because of the one who subjected it—in hope

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that the creation itself will also be set free from slavery to decay into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together and suffering birth pains together until now.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit—we too groan within ourselves as we wait for adoption, the redemption of our bodies.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For in this hope we were saved. But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what they see?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with endurance.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same way the Spirit also helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with wordless groans,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he who searches hearts knows what the mindset of the Spirit is, because the Spirit intercedes for the holy ones as God wills.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For those he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he would be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And those he predestined he also called; and those he called he also justified; and those he justified he also glorified.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all—how will he not also, along with him, freely give us all things?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Who will bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? It is God who justifies.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Who is the one who will condemn? Christ is the one who died—or rather, who was raised—who is also at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Affliction or distress or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “For your sake we are being put to death all day long; we were considered as sheep for slaughter.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I am convinced that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: nor height nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

notes.note: The manuscripts are divided between “you” (singular), “me” and, in a few, “us.” The edition translated here reads “you”; “me” continues the first-person voice of chapter 7 and is found in many manuscripts and in older English versions. The sense of the argument is the same either way.

The Greek is literally “and concerning sin.” In the Greek Old Testament this exact phrase is the regular expression for the sin offering, and many scholars think Paul’s readers would have heard it that way. Others take it more generally as “to deal with sin,” and many translations render it simply “for sin.”

notes.traditional: to be carnally minded / the mind set on the flesh
notes.note: The Greek noun names a settled way of thinking, an outlook or orientation, and is related to the verb translated “set their minds on” in verse 5. Traditional versions paraphrase it with a verb or render it “mind”; “mindset” keeps it a noun and is used again in verse 27 for the Spirit’s own intention.

Greek manuscripts did not distinguish capital letters, so the word can mean God’s Spirit or the human spirit. Many translations take it as the human spirit, “your spirit is alive.” Paul’s word is the noun “life,” not “alive,” and the surrounding verses speak throughout of God’s Spirit as the giver of life, so that reading is followed here; the question remains disputed.

notes.phrase: because of his Spirit who dwells in you
notes.traditional: through his Spirit who dwells in you
notes.note: The manuscripts differ by a grammatical case ending: some read “because of his Spirit,” others “through his Spirit.” The edition translated here prints the first; most English versions follow the second. Both readings are ancient, and the difference is whether the indwelling Spirit is the reason for the resurrection or its agent.

The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women as fellow members of a family, and Paul is writing to the whole community. “Brothers” alone now suggests to English readers that only men are addressed. Many recent translations make the same choice.

This was the ordinary Greek term for legal adoption, a practice familiar in the Roman world, in which the adopted son received the full status and inheritance rights of an heir. That background explains the move from “sons” to “heirs” in verses 14–17. “Sons” is kept in verses 14 and 19 to preserve this link and the link with God’s own Son; it includes women and men alike, as “children” in verses 16–17 shows.

“Abba” is the Aramaic word for “father,” used in addressing God, and Paul sets the Greek word for “father” beside it. The same double form appears in Jesus’s prayer in Mark 14:36 and in Galatians 4:6, which suggests that Greek-speaking believers kept the Aramaic word from Jesus’s own way of praying. The popular claim that it means “Daddy” is not supported by the evidence; it was used by adults as well as children.

notes.traditional: groanings which cannot be uttered / groanings too deep for words
notes.note: The Greek adjective can mean “unspoken, without words” or “unable to be put into words.” The traditional renderings take the second sense; “wordless” leaves both open. The “groans” echo the groaning of creation and of believers in verses 22–23.

Paul uses this word for all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament’s language for Israel. “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue, which is not the meaning. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

notes.phrase: all things work together for good
notes.traditional: all things work together for good
notes.note: The Greek can be read with “all things” as the subject, as here, or with God as an unstated subject: “he works all things together for good” or “in all things he works for good.” Some early manuscripts make this explicit by adding “God” as the subject. Either way Paul’s point is that God’s purpose, not circumstance itself, secures the good outcome.

The Greek word was an ordinary term for hardship or oppression that presses on a person. “Tribulation” is now often heard as the name of a specific end-time period, which says more than the Greek does. “Affliction” is itself an old rendering of the word, and “distress” is kept for the different Greek word that follows.

Listed between angels and powers, “rulers” here most likely refers to spiritual beings thought to hold authority in the unseen world, not to human governments, though some interpreters include both. “Powers” later in the verse belongs to the same vocabulary. “Height” and “depth” may simply mean the farthest reaches of space, or may be terms for the regions such powers were thought to inhabit; this is uncertain.

candidates.reason: Paul’s use ranges from the physical body to human nature in opposition to God, and versions vary between “flesh,” “sinful nature” and “human nature,” so one policy is needed across the letters.
The plural as an address to mixed communities occurs throughout the letters and Acts, and the choice between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters” should be uniform.
Versions alternate between “patience,” “endurance,” “perseverance” and “steadfastness” for this recurring virtue, and readers should see the same word throughout.

The traditional “predestine” carries heavy later theological associations, and the six occurrences (Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, Ephesians) should be rendered alike whether it is kept or replaced by “decide beforehand.”
The word recurs in the Gospels, Paul, 1 Peter and Revelation, and the choice between “elect” and “chosen” should not vary from book to book.

warnings: Verse 32: παραδίδωμι is not rendered with a register form (hand over; hand on; hand down; give up; give over; entrust; risk; be ripe) and has no register-exception note.
